chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah al-Barqi, from Ibn Sinan, from Mansur al-Sayqal, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And the marriage of ownership of the right hand continues to the end of the chapter.
This is indicated by the saying of the Exalted: "And those who guard their private parts. Except from their wives or those their right hands possess, for indeed, they will not be blamed."
So the Exalted made permissible by the apparent meaning of the wording, the marriage of ownership of the right hand.
Then indeed, ownership occurs through various means, among them purchase, among them gift, and among them inheritance, according to the diversity of the modes of acquisition.
And when a man has young children and they have female slaves, it is permissible for him to appraise one of them for himself and have intercourse with her.
This is indicated by what he narrated:

key_terms.الْهَاشِمِيَّةُ: The Hashimiyyah (referring to the clan of Hashim, often implying status or specific rulings)
key_terms.نِكَاحُ مِلْكِ الْأَيْمَانِ: Marriage of ownership of the right hand (marrying a female slave)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling on a man marrying his own female slave?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi contextualizes this narration by linking the permissibility of marrying one's own slave (milk al-yaman) to the explicit allowance in Surah Al-Mu’minun, distinguishing it from temporary marriage (mut'ah) mentioned in the preceding text. He elaborates that ownership arises through various legal means such as purchase, gift, or inheritance, and specifically permits a father to marry one of his young daughters if he owns her, illustrating the flexibility of domestic slavery within Shia jurisprudence.
